segment.text: 「まア、おとなしくしていなよ」ひそかに自分で自分を制しながら、相手の顔を見ていた。この人は高見といって、一二度ある催しに自分を招いてくれた人で、人のよさそうな黙笑をその少し酔いの出た、そして睡そうなあの顔に続けている。「おい、小奈良の小大仏」と喉まで出たが、朋輩の者でもない人にと思って、ぐッと呑みこんでしまった。それから、さし障りのないと思えた言葉がべらべらと飛びだした。「もう、一杯すみました、な――この不景気に先生はなかなか景気がよさそうじゃアございませんか？　少しあやかりてい、な、――えい？　わたくしなぞはこれから自宅へ帰って、やッと――その、な――熱いのにありつけるかと思ってますのでげすが、な、かかアがその用意をしてあるかどうかも分りません」

sentences.text: 「まア、おとなしくしていなよ」ひそかに自分で自分を制しながら、相手の顔を見ていた。
この人は高見といって、一二度ある催しに自分を招いてくれた人で、人のよさそうな黙笑をその少し酔いの出た、そして睡そうなあの顔に続けている。
「おい、小奈良の小大仏」と喉まで出たが、朋輩の者でもない人にと思って、ぐッと呑みこんでしまった。
それから、さし障りのないと思えた言葉がべらべらと飛びだした。
「もう、一杯すみました、な――この不景気に先生はなかなか景気がよさそうじゃアございませんか？
少しあやかりてい、な、――えい？
わたくしなぞはこれから自宅へ帰って、やッと――その、な――熱いのにありつけるかと思ってますのでげすが、な、かかアがその用意をしてあるかどうかも分りません」

segment.text: 人の笑いさえ聞えれば、自分には気持ちよく響くのであるが、自分自身には少しもおもしろくないのが不思議であった。芸人としての理窟を言えば、それはたくさんあることはある。人を笑わせるには自分から笑っていては利き目がないということもその一つだ。けれども、自分は人の好む酒をもさし控えて、この商売に使う自分の声を保護しているくせに、人に向ってはやッぱり酒を呑むかのごとく見せかけなければならぬ。こんな苦しいことが他の仕事にもあろうか？　人は芸人なんてしゃアしゃアして、世に苦労もないように思ってるが、その本人にもなってみるがいい。人の知らない苦労をこてこてとしている。自分なんかはまるで苦労の固まりでもってできたような人間である。

芸人としての理窟を言えば、それはたくさんあることはある。
人を笑わせるには自分から笑っていては利き目がないということもその一つだ。
けれども、自分は人の好む酒をもさし控えて、この商売に使う自分の声を保護しているくせに、人に向ってはやッぱり酒を呑むかのごとく見せかけなければならぬ。
こんな苦しいことが他の仕事にもあろうか？
人は芸人なんてしゃアしゃアして、世に苦労もないように思ってるが、その本人にもなってみるがいい。
人の知らない苦労をこてこてとしている。
自分なんかはまるで苦労の固まりでもってできたような人間である。

segment.text: それでも、一つ楽みなことには、自分の長屋住いのうら垣根をぶん抜いて、そこから出たところの明き地を前々から安く借りて、野菜を作っている。そして多くできた時は、自分の家族がそれを喰うばかりでなく、隣り近所のものにも分配してやる。近所のものが喜ぶのを見るだけでもまた一つの楽みである。

segment.text: 小かぶや大根の葉につく青虫や黒虫は、畝並みに溝を掘っておいて、そこへ向って葉を振うと、皆ころころと落ちてしまう。それを一どきに踏みつけたり、子供なぞ棒の先で突ッついたりして、殺すのである。

segment.text: 昨今は胡瓜や茄子の苗をも植えつけたので、根切り虫に注意してやらねばならぬ。この虫は泥棒や自分たちと同様、夜業ばかりする奴だから、昼間探しても少しだッて姿を見せぬ。今夜はひとつ、晩飯をすませるとすぐ、自分はふんどし一つになり、子供に提灯を持たせて畑に行き、十分に根切り虫の退治をやってやろうと考えられた。

segment.text: 「………」この本読みを聴いて猫八はえらいところへ飛びこんできたものだと思われた。この思いは自分でも少しおおげさな考えだとは承知しながら、まるで自分の事を言われているようであった。自分には男の子が四人あって、総領は十四で高等一年、次ぎは十二で尋常五年、いずれも出来がよくて級長をしている。この十二のが父親の真似が上手で、しかも父親以上の芸を持ってるが、それでも第二の猫八にはしたくないのである。否、父親が猫の喧嘩や動物の声を真似して、高座のうえから客の機嫌を取ってるところを子供に見せたくないためにこそ、早くからわざわざこんな不便な郊外を選んで住んでるのだ。猫が虎に変っても、そこにたいした相違はない。

segment.text: 「そうれ見たまえ。みごとに白状に及んだじゃないかね、しかし虎を見たいんならわざわざ動物園まで行くにも及ぶまいぜ。――一二升飲ませれゃ誰だってなりますが？――どうだい、そッちの虎を見に行こうじゃないか？――そいつアいけません。何しろこいつを撒くわけには行きませんからね、と彼はまた子供をかえりみた。というところもあるのだが」と、主人はなお本を見い見い語って行った。そして皆が猫八などのいるのを忘れて虎の方へ心を傾けたが、猫八にはその虎が自分のようであった。「ばかさ加減を言えば由井の役だッて同じようなものさ。むしろ君の虎一役が名誉かもしれんぜ、人気が虎の一身に集まったりして、ね。――そう思ってわたくしも一生懸命やるだけはやるつもりなんですが、ね。――そうとも、僕たちだッてむしろ君の虎に期待しているよ。――恐れ入ります、と深井は苦笑をしながらも、内心少からず慰められた」

segment.text: 「………」猫八はそれでもこの最後の泣き合いの一件を聴くにいたってびッくり仰天をしたほどに目を見張ってみせた。これもやはりわざと誇張してみせた表情だとは自分ながら知らないでもなかったが、同時にわれ知らず、いつもは心の奥にのみ秘めていた物が顔にまで現われた気がしたというのは、自分の職業に対する悲しみと次男を第二の猫八にさせようかどうかという惑いとが一ときに誘いだされたからである。彼は自分の滑稽商売にも似合わぬ顔つきを人には見せたくないと努めているのだが、努めれば努めるほど顔その物が反対に言うことをきかなくなって、鏡にでも映してみれば、自分の顔がべそ掻き面になってるように思われた。が、もう、それを取り繕うことをしないで素直に、「いや感心いたしました」と、その小説が一座の作その物ででもあるかのように敬意を表した。「わたくしにも同じような悲哀がございまして、いかにも感心いたしました。けれども、もしわたくしにも、その、先生方のおしになる批評と申すのを一つ言わせていただきますと、その深井というのが自分の本意でない役を演じながら、それを子供に見せておいたのははなはだしい間違いだと思われますが――？」

segment.text: 「やはり、一種の結論でしょう、な」これは猫八には先に虎のお終いでちょッと言い損ないをしたと思えた、その取り返しのつもりであった。「ところが、これが宮様がたなどへ招かれてまいりますていと、ぎゃぎゃぎゃアなんて」と、突然歯をむきだし、目を躍らせ、顔を珍妙にしがめて、猫の喧嘩する時の様子をしてみせ、皆を一度に吹きださしめた。が、自分はすまして、言葉を続けた、「庭鳥じゃアない、猫の蹴合いをお見せ申すにはまだ差し支えはございません。先様が御婦人である場合などには、やんごとなきお顔をお隠しになる扇の影からもそのお笑いがよく伺われます。が、時によりますと、――○○○様へあがった時などは、お前は物真似ばかりでなく、落語というものも巧みだそうだから、ひとつおもしろいのをお客さま方にお聴かせ申せと言われましたので、わたくしはお断りいたしました。とても畏れ多くてできません。けれども、たってと言われたので、一席願いましたことは願いましたが、――妙なもので、初手から少しもお分りになりません。どうせわたくしどもはわたくしどもの劣等な社会の事しか存じませんから、自然その話もそこへ落ちます。――おい、八公、いたか」と言って、尻を捲くって上り框へ腰かける様子をしてみせ、「これがそもそも何の事だか通じないのですから、――べらんめい裸じゃア尻は捲くれねいから、な、なんていう気を利かしたおもしろ味も通じません。失礼な申し分ではございますが、まったく張り合いがない、どッと来べきところをでも皆様がたはおすましになっておられます」

segment.text: こう思って、自分は自分らの裏長屋の事を心に浮べていた。とッつきが怠けがちの鍛冶屋で、いつもその山の神に怒鳴られてる。その次ぎが女髪結いで、男が何人代ったか分らない。その隣りが自分の家で、そのまた次ぎには電車の車掌がいて、人のまだよく眠ってる時からがたッぴしやりだして、ちんちん屋の商売に出て行きゃアがる。そしてどん詰りには、目ッかちで跛足の蜆屋がいる。夏は皆ほとんど真ッ裸かの社会であるが、そのうちでも人間らしいのはまず自分のところばかりだ。百姓はほんの自分の片手間仕事だが、それでもそこにあのがりがり妄者どもの知らぬ余裕がある。そして大根や菜ッ葉をも時々は彼らにただ分配してやってる。これでも自分らは宵越しの金は持たぬちゃきちゃきの江戸ッ子で、自分は芸者の腹から浅草の有名な料理屋に生れ、女房も神田上水に産湯を使ったものだ。ついでに自分の見識を皆の前に披露したくなった。

segment.text: 「ある時、わたくしの長屋の入り口に立派な馬車が停りました。どうせまずい生活をしているのは御承知であったでげしょうが、――猫八と申す芸人の家はこちらか？――へいと、わたくしはちょッと当惑いたしました。――では、本人は在宅かどうか？――へい、師匠は今湯にまいって留守ですが――まさか、ふんどし一つのわたくしがその本人ですとは出られませんから、な。――ちょッとお待ちを願います、ただ今すぐ呼んでまいりますから――と言ってひとまずそとへ出ました。女房にはちょッと目くばせいたしましたが、気まずい顔をしておりました。――わたくしは家を出るていと、すぐ入り口の鍛冶屋へはいり、そこのかみさんに訳を話して衣物と帯とを持ってきてもらいまして、今湯から帰ってきた風をして、借りた手拭いを水に濡らしたのと石鹸箱とを持って、――お待たせいたしました、すみません、わたくしが猫八ですが、御用は？――弟子と師匠とが少しも顔が違ってませんから、向うも不思議に思ったのは止むを得ません。――じつは、○○家から来たのだが、同家ではただ今お前の話が出て、おもしろい芸をする者だそうだからすぐ来るように言ってこいとのことだが、と言うのでした」

segment.text: この時、近眼があまり遅くなると困るからと言って席を立った。その横顔をじろりと見上げて、自分は少し不愉快の意を表したけれども、彼は気がつかなかった。その上に、また他の二人も立って、いっしょに帰って行ったのである。これが寄席なら、どうせ木戸銭はすんでるものだからという諦めもつきやすい。けれども人がせっかく心を落ちつけて正直に語り続けているその中途で失敬して行くのは、本統の失敬ではないかと思えて、諦めがつきかねた。途中の暗い横丁から化けてでてやるぞと言ってやりたかったが、主人を初め、まだ熱心な相手が残ってるので話の調子はさほど折れもしなかった。

segment.text: 廃兵院で鶴の啼く声が澄みわたってよく聞える午前の一時近くになって、皆が席を立った。自分もわざと潔く立って、皆といっしょに二階を下りたが、ふところへねじこんだ古雑誌と菓子や煎餅の残物とが今夜のお礼代りかと思えば、ばかばかしいような気もして、ここでひそかに例の虎と抱き合ってしばらく何だか泣いてみたかった。けっして金の貰えないのをくよくよ思ってるわけでないのは、自分が江戸ッ子たる点に照り合わせても分ってるが、――そしてこれも江戸ッ子たる女房が、女の弱い気に負けて、時々よい越しの金を残そうとするのを、自分が投ぐりつけてまで使わせてしまうところを見てもらっても、分ってるが、――百姓の労働生活に比べてみると、自分は人にくだらない芸などを見せてそれで生活をしなければならぬ身が、今さらに何となく悲しかった。

chapter_summaries.0: 一. On the tram home reading Kōdan Club, Nekohachi is hailed by patron Takami. Passengers become an audience; he answers a Sugamo joke with a madmen-and-monsters quip, swallows a fat joke, then drifts into comedian's苦労, protecting his voice by not drinking, and allotment pests including night-working cutworms. Takami invites him to a writers' study group; worried about seedlings, he follows, rheumatic and limping.

hard_spots.why_hard: シチュエイション, バック/ハイケイ, ゲンジツシュギ, グタイ/クウタイ arrive as sound. Nekohachi guesses situation is a fix he is trapped in and compromise is flattery; he hears background as pure noise and thinks of konnyaku mondō. Translating them into smooth English criticism erases the joke and his truer misuse.
He keeps asking a novel for an ochi/conclusion as if it were rakugo. The group laughs at the wrong place. English must keep punchline/fall without explaining rakugo or making him knowing.

Half the night is second-hand Kume retold by the host, interrupted and judged thin. Polishing it into a moving tale betrays its flat reported texture and makes Nekohachi's recognition look disproportionate.
Nightingale, valley-crossing, crickets, cranes, frogs (くッくッ, かッかッ, けきょ), earthworm vs mole-cricket lore. They must read as act, with the room's thin laughter left thin, not as nature writing.
○○○様, ○○家, ○○子爵 are in the source as discretion about lords. Filling them, footnoting guesses, or smoothing to a certain lord removes the performed knowing-how-to-behave.

Tao Yuanming's return, Sanba as praise, konnyaku mondō as cover for not understanding. Each is Nekohachi dignifying incomprehension or the wish to leave; footnotes must be minimal and never award him the point.

でげす, な, beranmei, 大山大将, Kōdan Club, Sugamo madhouse, Yoshiwara embankment, rickety suburban allotment, petitioned gas lamp. Requires dropped run-on colloquial syntax without Cockney or stage-Japanese, and inventory without lyricism.

motifs.english: Keep one plain English set for the plot-work and do not vary: ditch, ridge, caterpillar/worm, seedling/root, cucumber, eggplant/aubergine. The garden is his competence and his alibi at every pressure point.
source_forms: 畑, 明き地, 野菜, 畝並み, 溝, 青虫, 黒虫, 根切り虫, 苗, 根, 小かぶ, 大根, 胡瓜, 茄子, 枳殻垣
motifs.why: Returns whenever money, art or sons press him; the only generosity nobody applauds and the farewell gift he presses on the gentlemen. Varying it dissolves Berman's network.

motifs.english: Keep the catalogue unvaried and unlyrical: tiger, cat, frog, monkey, pig, boar?/crane/nightingale/cricket/mole-cricket/earthworm, aeroplane/motorcar, firefly/colic-worm. Let tiger stay tiger, frog stay frog.
source_forms: 虎, 猫, 化け物, かわず, 猿, 豚, 鶯, 松虫, 鈴虫, 轡虫, 烏, ひばり, うずら, おけら, 鶴, 草ひばり, 蚯蚓, 螢, 疝気の虫, 飛行器, 自動車
motifs.why: Runs from the opening Sugamo joke through frog-origin to tiger-monkey-pig farewell. It is labour, evasion and identification at once; elegant variation would moralise it.

motifs.english: Keep child/children/sons and the fixed phrase second Nekohachi identical each time; keep the ages flatly stated.
motifs.motif: children and the dreaded second Nekohachi
source_forms: 子供, 子, 家族, 男の子が四人, 総領, 次男, 第二の猫八
motifs.why: His suburban exile, his condemnation of Fukai for showing the child, and his delight at being known all turn on this. Softening it into fatherly love settles what the story leaves double.

motifs.english: Keep money words blunt and repeated: fee, wooden gate charge, contribution, two yen coins, overnight money. Do not euphemise the fretting.
motifs.motif: fee that must not be named

motifs.english: Keep hiai as sorrow/grief unvaried once adopted; keep situation/background/compromise/personality/concrete as English-derived abstractions set against his patter, with his misuses left visible.
motifs.motif: borrowed critical words: hiai, situation, background
source_forms: 悲哀, シチュエイション, バック, ハイケイ/背景, 妥協/譲歩, 皮肉, 人物, 人格的生活, 具体的, 現実主義, 理想主義
motifs.why: The action is a language collision. He learns hiai across the room and carries it home as pay; he mouths situation/background without parsing them. Merging the two Englishes kills the tension.

motifs.english: Keep madman/monster/beast-fool wording stable; keep teasing/heckling/fooling and compromise/flattery wording stable.

motifs.why: Opening joke that only madmen and monsters live in Sugamo quietly tests the whole night: who fools whom, audience or actor. Do not upgrade into irony or villainy.

narration.english_tense: Past as default for narrated action and interior slide; keep present only where Japanese stage directions or gnomic asides demand it. Do not hop tenses to manufacture climax at p175 or p185.
narration.frame: One evening's drift: tram ride home from two engagements, two-hour writers' meeting, midnight walk to a suburban row-house gate. Flash memories (candy-selling, frog discovery, lord visits) surface inside that drift without chapter breaks beyond the seven numbered cuts.
narration.narrator: Close third person glued to Nekohachi; slides into his idiom, jokes and self-justifications without endorsing or correcting them. Even at the most abject admissions (wife-beating, fee-shame) the tone stays dogged and garrulous.
narration.person: third person, internally focalised on Nekohachi
narration.tense_habits: Japanese moves freely between past recollection, present-tense stagey aside, and gnomic summary; subjects drop for stretches and speakers go unattributed. English must tolerate long associative sentences and delayed attribution rather than rationalising them.
timeline: afternoon-evening: tram home after two kōza, heckle and tram reverie (p2-p21)
street meeting with stout woman, walk to house (p22-p35)
upstairs study group: Tiger paraphrase and verdicts (p37-p100)
Kume self-review debate, student exchange, side talk with hostess (p102-p120)
demand to perform: mimicry set and frog-origin story (p122-p159)
three leave mid-story; fee talk, pig-farming digression, hunger (p161-p173)
near 1 a.m.: dispersal, two yen outside, gate farewell, walk to door planning to retell it to wife (p175-p188)

part_summaries.summary: 一. On the tram home reading Kōdan Club, Nekohachi is hailed by patron Takami. Passengers become an audience; he answers a Sugamo joke with a madmen-and-monsters quip, swallows a fat joke, then drifts into comedian's苦労, protecting his voice by not drinking, and allotment pests including night-working cutworms. Takami invites him to a writers' study group; worried about seedlings, he follows, rheumatic and limping.

二. They enter a house with a cucumber plot and climb to six or seven writers. Introduced as the famous Nekohachi, he charms and apologises for rheumatism. The host, a bathhouse acquaintance, begins the absent T-kun's agenda item: Kume's Tiger from May Bunsho Sekai. The paraphrase of a comic actor given only a beast's part hits Nekohachi as his own life with four sons and a gifted twelve-year-old he keeps from the yose.

三. The paraphrase continues through zoo research, a sharp critic, applause for a yawn and leap. Nekohachi misuses situation to protest the compromise and is ignored. The ending is told: after the ovation the costumed father finds his small son weeping in the dark wings and tiger and human child weep together. Nekohachi, half-performing grief, objects that Fukai should never have let the child see it and tells of hiding his own sons in the suburbs.

四. The group calls Tiger thin and backgroundless. The Tenjin-like man reveals Kume himself wrote the savage anonymous Jiji Shinpō review; Nekohachi takes Kume for a Sanba-like wit and says the audience decides. A silent student asks about personality backing work; host and others answer with concrete/abstract jargon Nekohachi hears as konnyaku mondō. Talk drifts; hostess gives him cakes and children's magazines; Takami calls for a performance.

五. Triumphant in his own world, he does caged and valley nightingales, crickets, crows, mole-crickets, cranes, and earthworm lore that once got him taken for a burglar. Asked for his motive, he tells the candy-seller origin: rheumatism, failed peddling, frog sexes distinguished on the Yoshiwara bank, then sales. Warned against vulgarisation, he defends fooling audiences, mimics a cat fight, and tells failed upper-house visits with borrowed kimono and blanked lordly names.

六. Three including the near-sighted man leave mid-story; Nekohachi resents it as true rudeness. Fee pride is debated: he will not name a price yet will go free if moved. Pig-farming talk excludes him; hungry and bored, he frets over who pays, talks gardens with the hostess to cover his face, and eats more cakes.

七. Near 1 a.m. by the waste-hospital forest they disperse. Pockets stuffed with old magazines and cake leavings as fee, he wants to embrace the tiger and weep. Takami quietly slips him two yen; ashamed of relief and wanting to quit, he sees them off, advertises cucumbers and eggplants at his dark gate, and goes to his door past sleeping rows to retell the novel to his wife.

body.say: Keep Nekohachi's working patter and the writers' borrowed abstractions as two unblended Englishes; keep the Tiger paraphrase flat and the garden inventory serious; let his borrowed sorrow stay learned, performed and real at once without resolving him into victim or butt.

style_sheet.annotation_density: Sparse. Annotate only what the sentence cannot give: yose/kōza, Kōdan Club, Sugamo madhouse, shinpa, Tao Yuanming, Sanba, konnyaku mondō if kept. Never gloss what context supplies or explain his misunderstandings in-text.
style_sheet.author_voice: Taishō naturalist inventory: dogged, repetitive, faintly garrulous even when sad; long associative slides; lists of food, pests, coins, cries. Do not lyricise the sad passages or brisk up the comic ones; the bathos at p175 and the rare humility at p185 must read at the same temperature as the tram jokes.
style_sheet.honorifics_and_names: Japanese order surname-first for Japanese names. Keep Sensei for Nekohachi's address to Takami and others because the relation lives in it; keep -san/-kun/-sama where socially load-bearing (Takami-san, Nekohachi-san/Kun, Tenjin-sama as nickname). Romanise with macrons: Nekohachi, Takami, Kume, Tō Enmei, Fukai.
style_sheet.keep_in_japanese: Keep Sensei, yose, kōza, and the English-derived loanwords as situation/background where the joke is mouthing English; keep ochi as fall/punchline glossed once if needed. Keep blanked names as blanks (Mr ___, the ___ house) not filled.
style_sheet.quotation: Use single quotes for quoted Tiger paraphrase inside host speech where needed; double quotes for direct speech. Keep the group's thin laughter as ha, ha, ha without upgrading to roars.
style_sheet.register: Two audible Englishes, never merged: Nekohachi in dropped, run-on, self-interrupting colloquial patter with verbal tics for な/でげす, competent about gardens and mimicry; writers in flat borrowed critical abstraction. Neither polished into the same literary fluency.
style_sheet.ruby_and_italics: No ruby in English. Italicise only loanwords kept as Japanese and titles of works/magazines (Tiger, Bunso Sekai, Kōdan Club) on first use; otherwise roman.

english: "Oi, boss," came the call, and Nekohachi lifted his eyes from the Koudan Club he had been buried in and turned them toward the voice. He knew by the voice who it was, and that put him at his ease,
"Well, Sensei!" putting on a vacant look on purpose. "Fancy meeting you on this tram, eh? So then, some fine nest has turned up round this way, eh?"

"..." That got him straight off, one down. But by now all the passengers around were pricking up their ears, so he called back into himself the feeling from the kouza he had just come off with his hands free. And with all the passengers starting to look like his own customers to him, he felt here he would have to give something back somehow. "That would be it, eh," putting on a suddenly solemn face, and just then with a sidelong glance catching their tram passing in front of the lunatic hospital he made it into material,
"In a place like Sugamo there is nothing living but madmen or monsters like Nekohachi, eh."

"ha, ha, ha," somebody laughed, and so even in a place like this he got the response he always got. He thought of the place and tried to hold back any further wisecracks on top of it, but somehow his mouth seemed unwilling to agree to it.
takes.label: close, warm, and performed - the house recommendation
takes.line: Narration in plain, slightly long-winded English that keeps slipping into Nekohachi's own turn of phrase without quotation marks or apology; it reports his self-flatteries (Edo-born, money never kept overnight) in the same tone as his seedlings, and never steps back to judge either. Nekohachi himself in dropped, wheedling, run-on speech, all apologies and 'now, look here' and sentence-final appeals for agreement, quickening into pure act - sound-words, animal cries, abrupt changes of face - when he performs; his seriousness should keep breaking the patter rather than replacing it. The literati in complete, abstract, faintly bored sentences, polysyllabic where he is monosyllabic, kind in the way of people who will not be there at the end of the sentence. Takami a register between: clubbable, easy, the only man who speaks both languages. Wrong for this take: dialect spelling, music-hall Cockney, 'gee' and 'ain't' folksiness, or any lyric lift at the tiger's climax - the moment the English gets beautiful, it has joined the study group against him.

english: "Hey, boss," he was hailed, and Nekohachi turned his eyes from the Kodan Club he had been buried in toward the voice. He knew by the voice right away who it was, so he felt at ease,
"Well, Sensei!" he said, putting on a vacant face on purpose, "we do keep meeting on this tram, now. So a fine nest has turned up for you out this way, eh?"
"What, the nest at Sugamo, that's all!"

He was floored straight off by that. But by now the passengers all around were pricking up their ears, so he pulled back into his heart the feeling from the koza he had just come up from with his hands now free. And the passengers all began to look like his own audience, so he felt he had got to give something back somehow. "I daresay, eh," he said, putting on a suddenly solemn face, and just then, glancing to see their tram passing in front of the madhouse, he made material of it,
"Out in a place like Sugamo there is nothing living but madmen or monsters like Nekohachi, eh."

"Ha, ha, haa," somebody laughed, so even in such a place he got his usual response in a way, but when he thought of the place and tried to hold back any further light talk on top of it, somehow his mouth seemed unwilling to agree.
takes.label: drier and more naturalist
takes.line: Narration flatter and cooler, closer to reportage, letting the inventories of the tenement, the allotment and the evening's talk accumulate without warmth, so that Nekohachi's bursts of patter stand out as noise he makes against a quiet world. His speech still colloquial but less lovable - more repetitive, more importunate - and the literati barely differentiated from one another, a single murmur of educated dismissal. This take risks seeming to side with the room, but it honours Iwano's naturalism and makes the final walk home colder and less consoling. Wrong for it: any softening of the wife-beating admission or the fee anxiety, which this take needs unglossed to work.

english: 'Hey, boss,' he was hailed, and Nekohachi lifted his eyes from the Kodan Club he had been buried in till now. He knew at once from the voice who it was, so he felt at ease.
'Well now, Sensei!' he said, putting on a blank look for it. 'We keep meeting on this tram, don't we — so then, some nice little nest turned up for you out this way, eh?'

... That got him, clean, right away. But just about then all the passengers around were pricking up their ears, so he dragged back up inside himself the feel from the koza he had just come off, with time on his hands now. And the passengers all began to look like his own audience, so here he felt he had got to get something back somehow. 'That is right, I suppose, eh,' he said, putting on a sudden solemn face, and just then catching with a sidelong glance that their tram was passing right in front of the asylum he worked it straight into his material: 'Out in a place like Sugamo there is nothing living, eh, but madmen or monsters like Nekohachi.'

'ha, ha, ha,' somebody laughed, so even in a place like this he got, after a fashion, the response he always got. He thought of where he was and tried to hold back any more lip on top of that, but somehow his mouth seemed unwilling to agree.
takes.label: more theatrical, playing the act
takes.line: Narration keeps pace with a performer thinking: quicker cuts, jokes left to land or die in the spacing, the animal imitations given real stage room with their onomatopoeia carried over, and the study-group scenes played almost as dialogue in a play, Nekohachi a comic turn among tragedians. His origin story on the Yoshiwara embankment becomes the bravura centre it is in his own mind. This take is the most readable aloud and the most dangerous: it flatters exactly the gift the story is examining, and will need discipline to keep the garden passages, the walkouts and the two yen as heavy as the applause. Wrong for it: punchlines sharpened beyond the source, or pathos borrowed back from the tiger to pay for the comedy.

options.author: first read (Wonder)
options.case:
- keep Nekohachi's patter as work, not local colour His banter on the tram in p2-p10 is not decoration before the serious part begins; it is the act itself, carried on in public because passengers have become an audience and a comeback is professionally compulsory. Again at the meeting he tests jokes, misapplies the borrowed word "situation" (p67-p69), apologises, recovers, and feels the flatness when は、は、は does not come (p63). If English tidies this into witty repartee it ennobles him; if it renders it as broad dialect comedy it does to him exactly what his audiences do. For the English: he must never become quaint Cockney or stage-Japanese. Use dropped, run-on, self-interrupting colloquial syntax, repetitions and verbal tics in place of the sentence-ending な and the self-deprecating でげす forms, and let the dignity show through competence and generosity, not through making his grammar more respectable.
- keep the ramble, because the ramble is the consciousness The narration stays glued to Nekohachi's mind, and that mind does not proceed: on the tram it slides from a heckle to why a comedian must not laugh, to protecting a voice he does not drink for, to caterpillars in a ditch and cutworms that, like thieves and like himself, work only at night (p10-p14). The garden returns at every pressure point (p20, p31-p33, p100, p158, p172-p173) and is still what he offers the departing gentlemen at his own gate (p182). A fluent version that breaks this into themed paragraphs, or clarifies the transitions, has rationalised away the man. For the English: do not iron out the long, associative sentences in which cabbages, a bath, a fee and a son succeed one another, and do not cut the lists. options.case:
- The collision of languages is the action: close third-person narration saturated with Nekohachi's Edokko yose patter (でげす, な, self-deprecating jokes, internal 洒落 he performs even to himself) set against the literati's imported jargon (シチュエイション, バック, 現実主義/具体) that he literally cannot parse. He is never off stage—he swallows '小奈良の小大仏' (p8), turns a tram ride into a 高座 (p5-9), negotiates every humiliation as a gag—while they study that very compulsion as '悲哀' in Kume's '虎'. Strip the register gap and the plot (a mimic taken to a research society) has no tension left: his mishearings of 'situation' as a predicament he is trapped in (p53), his gratitude at being quoted back as criticism (p79-82), and his final triumph in performance (p124-136) all only register because we hear him thinking and speaking in a different tongue from theirs. - The mirrored tiger must stay unresolved: Nekohachi condemns Fukai for letting his child see the debasing role (p91-95) and has moved to the suburbs to hide his own, yet eagerly performs, fishes for praise and a fee (p171-177), and misreads Kume's anonymous self-denunciation as proof Kume is a wit after his own heart (p103-110). fork.question: Do the two readings name the same crux in different words, or different cruxes — Nekohachi's associative performed consciousness as the form to preserve, versus the unblended collision of his tongue with the literati's and the unresolved tiger-mirror as the structure to preserve? They share patter and 'The Tiger', but each makes central what the other leaves secondary, and adopting one will direct choices the other would direct differently, so the text does not settle it as mere rewording.

open_questions.question: How far to take Nekohachi's borrowed critical words? He picks up シチュエイション and uses it to mean something like a fix, then perhaps 'compromise' (p67-p69), asks after a novel's 落ち as if it were a rakugo punchline (p82), and hears バック/ハイケイ and こんにゃく問答 as pure sound (p118). Keeping the English words 'situation' and 'background' preserves the joke that he is mouthing English; explaining his misunderstandings in the text would clarify what the story leaves for the reader to infer.
open_questions.why_it_matters: This is where the class gap is audible. Over-explanation makes him stupid, under-explanation makes the passages merely opaque, and either choice decides how much the reader laughs at him rather than with him.

open_questions.question: What to do with the blanked names ○○○様 and ○○家 (p155, p159, p168)? The blanks are in the source: discretion about aristocratic patrons, performed in the telling. Silently filling, footnoting speculative identities, or smoothing them into 'a certain lord' would each change the effect; the blank itself is Nekohachi showing he knows how to behave in great houses.
open_questions.why_it_matters: The blanks mark the exact border between his world and the one that summons carriages for him. They are also part of his boasting: he has been to houses whose names must be withheld.

open_questions.question: How straight to play the revelation that Kume anonymously savaged his own story in a review (p103), which instantly converts Nekohachi into Kume's admirer (p104)? The group reads it as frivolity; Nekohachi reads it as 茶気, a performer's trick he recognises, and concludes the audience decides (p107-p108).
open_questions.why_it_matters: It is the one moment his professional judgement and the literati's may be pointing, from opposite sides, at the same thing. Playing it as simple irony rebukes him; playing it as simple insight rebukes them.

open_questions.question: Is the ending's humility (p185) a genuine change of heart, a mood of one in the morning that will not survive breakfast, or the last performance of the night, given to himself? He wants to embrace the tiger and weep (p175), is ashamed of his own relief at two yen (p177), and goes home resolved to make his wife taste an entertainer's sorrow (p188).
open_questions.why_it_matters: An English ending that resolves into renunciation or redemption betrays the text; so does one that undercuts him with open irony. The temperature of the last page is an editorial fork the reading cannot settle.

body.reading:
The crux of 『猫八』 is a man hearing his own life told back to him as somebody else's mediocre fiction, and being unable to say so in any language the room will accept. Nekohachi is a yose mimic, half-crippled by rheumatism for over a decade, who earns his living imitating cats fighting, birds, insects and latterly aeroplanes, and who has moved his family to an inconvenient suburb precisely so that his gifted twelve-year-old son will not watch him do it and will not become a second Nekohachi (p50, p95). Taken by the patron Takami to a writers' study group, he listens to a flat paraphrase of Kume's 「虎」, about a comic actor cast as a tiger, proud of the applause, and found after the curtain by his small son, crying in the costume: "the tiger and the human child wept together for a while in the shadow of the dark scenery" (p87). Everyone present agrees the piece is shallow, deft, thin in background. Nekohachi sits with one hand on the tatami and thinks it is about him. A translation stands or falls on whether that recognition lands without ever being upgraded into insight: he does not achieve self-knowledge in the story, he achieves a feeling - 悲哀, a word he has literally just learned from the man across the room (p56-p57) - and he carries it home past the sleeping tenement like something he has been paid in.

Everything follows from keeping the two registers unmerged. Nekohachi's spoken voice is Edo working patter: ingratiating, self-deprecating, built on な and でげす, forever turning a slight into a routine - the heckler on the tram must be answered because the other passengers have become an audience (p5-p10), the fat acquaintance must be greeted with 大山大将 and a lie about another engagement to save face (p23-p26), a lord's carriage must be met by borrowing a kimono from the blacksmith's wife and pretending to come back from the bath (p159). This is not colour; it is labour, and it is also evasion. Against it stands the literati's talk, abstract, loanworded and cool: シチュエイション, バック, 現実主義, 具体的, personality as the backing of a work (p103-p117). Nekohachi understands none of the terms and most of the substance. He thinks "situation" may mean a tight spot, which for him it does: he is はめられて, fitted into the patrons' favour until he can no longer move (p53). The translation must let the reader hear that he is misusing their words and meaning something truer with them, without a narrator stepping in to award him the point. Equally, the gentlemen must not be flattened into villains. They are mildly kind, mildly bored, they feed him餅菓子 instead of the drink he refuses, the host's wife talks gardens and children with him (p119-p120), Takami quietly presses two yen on him outside (p176) - and three of them walk out in the middle of the most honest story he ever tells (p161). Condescension here is structural, not snarling, and English that gives them sneers, or gives him a rebuttal, destroys it.

The narration is the third voice and the treacherous one, because it keeps slipping into Nekohachi's own idiom and self-justifications: the long tram reverie that moves from why a comedian must not laugh, to the voice he protects by not drinking, to green caterpillars shaken into a ditch and stamped on (p10-p13); the sudden boilerplate of Edo pride, no money kept overnight, born in Asakusa to a geisha mother (p158), set down right beside the admission that he beats his wife for trying to save (p175). The narrator neither endorses nor corrects any of this. That evenness is what a fluent draft will most want to fix, by making the interior passages lyrical where the story turns sad and brisk where it is comic. Resist it. The prose should stay dogged, repetitive and faintly garrulous even at p175, when he wants, in hiding, to embrace the tiger and weep for a while: the bathos is the emotion, and ennobling it into a climax would be the exact falsification the story is about.

Against the stage the text sets the allotment, and it must be translated as seriously as the tiger. Digging a ditch along the rows so the caterpillars roll in (p12), watching for cutworms that work nights as he does (p13), worrying on the tram home that two or three seedlings' roots will be cut before he gets back (p20), the surplus cucumbers and aubergines he gives away (p11, p182): this is the one place he is competent without being laughed at, and the one generosity nobody applauds. Note that he ends the evening not with a resolution to quit - he does wish, at p177, that he could stop tomorrow - but by advertising his vegetables to the departing writers at his own dark gate, and planning to make his wife taste what he has felt (p182-p188). The shape is a long evening that changes nothing except the temperature of a man's self-pity, and translations that sharpen it into an arc of awakening will have imported the 落ち he himself kept asking for and was laughed at for expecting (p82-p85).

Repetitions are load-bearing throughout: the animal catalogue that runs from tiger, monkey and pig (p179) through his frog-origin story (p141-p145) to the firefly and the colic-worm he cannot imitate and blusters about (p147-p153); the children and the dreaded second Nekohachi; the fee that must never be named and is always on his mind (p171, p175-p177); the 気違いか猫八のような化け物 of the opening joke (p6), madmen and monsters as the only residents of Sugamo, which the whole story quietly tests. Keep them unvaried. Keep his set-pieces - the caged nightingale, the valley-crossing, the mating cranes, the earthworm research that got him taken for a burglar (p62, p124-p130) - as performance, with the room's inadequate laughter left inadequate. And keep the unglamorous furniture: Kōdan Club magazine, the gas lamp he has petitioned to advertise himself with (p186), the leftover cakes in his pocket with the borrowed magazines. This is a Taishō naturalist story whose pity works by inventory, not by statement.
