voice_takes.label: close, warm, and performed - the house recommendation
voice_takes.line: Narration in plain, slightly long-winded English that keeps slipping into Nekohachi's own turn of phrase without quotation marks or apology; it reports his self-flatteries (Edo-born, money never kept overnight) in the same tone as his seedlings, and never steps back to judge either. Nekohachi himself in dropped, wheedling, run-on speech, all apologies and 'now, look here' and sentence-final appeals for agreement, quickening into pure act - sound-words, animal cries, abrupt changes of face - when he performs; his seriousness should keep breaking the patter rather than replacing it. The literati in complete, abstract, faintly bored sentences, polysyllabic where he is monosyllabic, kind in the way of people who will not be there at the end of the sentence. Takami a register between: clubbable, easy, the only man who speaks both languages. Wrong for this take: dialect spelling, music-hall Cockney, 'gee' and 'ain't' folksiness, or any lyric lift at the tiger's climax - the moment the English gets beautiful, it has joined the study group against him.

voice_takes.label: drier and more naturalist
voice_takes.line: Narration flatter and cooler, closer to reportage, letting the inventories of the tenement, the allotment and the evening's talk accumulate without warmth, so that Nekohachi's bursts of patter stand out as noise he makes against a quiet world. His speech still colloquial but less lovable - more repetitive, more importunate - and the literati barely differentiated from one another, a single murmur of educated dismissal. This take risks seeming to side with the room, but it honours Iwano's naturalism and makes the final walk home colder and less consoling. Wrong for it: any softening of the wife-beating admission or the fee anxiety, which this take needs unglossed to work.

voice_takes.label: more theatrical, playing the act
voice_takes.line: Narration keeps pace with a performer thinking: quicker cuts, jokes left to land or die in the spacing, the animal imitations given real stage room with their onomatopoeia carried over, and the study-group scenes played almost as dialogue in a play, Nekohachi a comic turn among tragedians. His origin story on the Yoshiwara embankment becomes the bravura centre it is in his own mind. This take is the most readable aloud and the most dangerous: it flatters exactly the gift the story is examining, and will need discipline to keep the garden passages, the walkouts and the two yen as heavy as the applause. Wrong for it: punchlines sharpened beyond the source, or pathos borrowed back from the tiger to pay for the comedy.

revision.english: "Oi, boss," came the call, and Nekohachi lifted his eyes from the Koudan Club he had been buried in and turned them toward the voice. He knew by the voice who it was, and that put him at his ease,
notes: "boss" for taishou, Takami's familiar hail. Koudan Club kept as magazine title.

revision.english: "Well, Sensei!" putting on a vacant look on purpose. "Fancy meeting you on this tram, eh? So then, some fine nest has turned up round this way, eh?"
notes: su as nest keeps the pun picked up in p4 with Sugamo no su. Sensei kept for Nekohachi's address to Takami. Second eh for sentence-final na.

revision.english: "What, a Sugamo nest, that's all!"

"..." That got him straight off, one down. But by now all the passengers around were pricking up their ears, so he called back into himself the feeling from the kouza he had just come off with his hands free. And with all the passengers starting to look like his own customers to him, he felt here he would have to give something back somehow. "That would be it, eh," putting on a suddenly solemn face, and just then with a sidelong glance catching their tram passing in front of the lunatic hospital he made it into material,
notes: kouza kept as stage. Long run-on kept as one pull back into performance because the passengers have become an audience. Tenkyou hospital as lunatic hospital in front of which the tram is passing.

revision.english: "In a place like Sugamo there is nothing living but madmen or monsters like Nekohachi, eh."
notes: Keeps third-person Nekohachi and madmen/monster wording stable as load-bearing repetition. eh for na.

revision.english: "ha, ha, ha," somebody laughed, and so even in a place like this he got the response he always got. He thought of the place and tried to hold back any further wisecracks on top of it, but somehow his mouth seemed unwilling to agree to it.
notes: Laughter kept thin as ha, ha, ha. Mouth unwilling keeps the compulsion to keep performing even while checking himself.

revision.english: "Now, now, keep yourself quiet, eh," he was telling himself under his breath as he looked at the other's face. This was Takami, who had asked him along once or twice for some affair, and he was keeping that good-natured silent grin going on his sleepy face with a touch of drink in it. "Oi, little Buddha of little Nara" came right up to his throat, but he gulped it back down, thinking the man was no fellow performer to say that to. Then what looked like harmless words came rattling out. "Had your one already, eh— things as dull as they are, Sensei looks to be doing pretty well for himself, eh? Let me have a bit of it, eh, what do you say? Me, I am off home now and if I am lucky, well, you know, I might get something hot, I suppose, eh, though whether the missus has got it ready or not I don't know."
notes: Swallowed retort left literal: 'little Buddha of little Nara' is Nekohachi's private nickname for Takami from girth and sleepy face, gulped back because Takami is no fellow performer. 'Missus' renders kakaa, his Edokko word for his own wife.

revision.english: "ha, ha, ha!" The man holding his seat across the way and staring this way laughed again.

So long as he heard people laughing it rang pleasant in him, and yet it was strange that there was nothing funny to himself at all. If you wanted the comedian's logic for it, there was plenty and to spare. That to make people laugh there is no effect in laughing yourself is one of them. And yet, though he held off even from the drink people like, to protect this voice he uses for the trade, when he faced people he still had to make it look as if he drank. Could there be such hardship in any other work. People think a comedian just breezes along with no troubles in the world, but let them try being the man himself. He is thick with troubles people know nothing of. A man like himself is as if made out of a lump of trouble.

Still, for one pleasure, he had pulled out the back fence of his row-house lodgings, and from there rented cheap from long back the open ground that lay beyond, and grew vegetables there. And when they came up plenty, not only did his own family eat them, he shared them out to the neighbours round about as well. Just to see the neighbours pleased was another pleasure in itself.

The green caterpillars and black worms that get on the leaves of little turnips and daikon, you dig a ditch along the ridges, and shake the leaves toward it, and they all come rolling down. Then you stamp them all at once, or the children prod them with the end of a stick, and kill them.
notes: Kept ditch, ridges, caterpillars and worms in the bible's plain set, and kept pleasure repeated in p11 as in the Japanese.

revision.english: Of late he had set out cucumber and eggplant seedlings as well, so the cutworms had to be watched. Like thieves, like people in our trade, the things do their work only by night, so hunt for them by day and you never see a sign of them. Tonight, he was thinking, the moment supper was done he would strip to his loincloth and have a child hold the lantern for him out in the field, and make a thorough job of doing for the cutworms.
notes: Kept cutworms and night work literal: the comparison to thieves and to us is the point that returns at p62 and p158, not decoration.

revision.english: Then the little-Buddha Sensei opened his eyes wide. "No more work tonight, I suppose?"
notes: Grouped in English as one paragraph: p14 is only the lead into the speech. Kept the private nickname as little-Buddha Sensei rather than explaining it.

revision.english: "Yes, I have got my two kouza behind me, but --" That did not feel like answer enough, so catching what the other was driving at, "Might I tag along with you somewhere tasty, eh?"
"Oh, if it is only home to bed for you, why not come along with me?"
"I will come -- on your orders, anywhere." Even to Kegon Falls, the song says -- the words came unbidden to his lips.
notes: Left the Kegon Falls song as heard: I could not settle which song he means, only that a set phrase about going anywhere has risen to his mouth.

revision.english: "It is a study group of writers, you know, no harm in listening a while. Come now and it is only two hours to stick out. Afterwards I will make it your world."
notes: Kept your world literal for o-mae no sekai: your turn, your stage, left for the reader to hear.

revision.english: "That sounds fun, eh, I'll come along too, to learn a thing or two, eh." He answered light enough, but he was fretting whether the load he had just set down would be loaded on his back again tonight. For him there was no time when body and mind felt lighter than in the tram on the way home after doing his union turn each night. From what he had heard he could not get home for at least another two or three hours. And in that time those cutworms might have cut through the roots of two or three of the seedlings in his plot, for all he knew.
notes: 後学のため is a polite self-deprecating formula. I have it as 'to learn a thing or two, eh' to keep his wheedling patter and the sentence-final appeal of な rather than a literal 'for future study'. The cutworm and seedling roots wording is kept the same as p13 to hold the garden network.

revision.english: With that worry on one side of his mind, the tram soon reached the terminus, so he stuffed the Kodan Club inside his coat and got up after Takami-san, carrying his crippled body hobble hobble toward the exit. For a dozen years and more now his rheumatism had left him all but palsied down one side. Crippled as no one else is, he was thankful, as the saying goes that art saves the man, that he could still keep wife and children fed like anyone else.
notes: ひょこりひょこり is his habitual movement word. I have it as 'hobble hobble' to keep the doubled sound without caricature. 芸が身を助ける is kept close as 'art saves the man' to keep the proverb flat, and 人並み is kept as 'as no one else / like anyone else' to keep the repetition.

revision.english: Walking along in silence he was apt to sink into earnest thoughts like these, when a fat woman he knew met him and broke them up again.
"Nekohachi-san!" Pushing her fat bulk on ahead of her as if proud of it, she called out to him as they passed, though she need not have, in a gentle voice that did not match the bulk, "Home now?"
notes: でぶでぶ女 and 太った図体 are body-first in the narration. I keep 'fat woman' and 'fat bulk' blunt and unvaried rather than softening it. 止せばいいのに is the narration sliding into his voice, so I keep it as a plain aside, 'though she need not have'.

revision.english: "Well, General Oyama!" He just had to tease again, so he teased as he always did. He turned sideways toward her and pulled himself up stiff and solemn to a stop, but she went off laughing, so he let her go out of his sight and chased her with words alone, "I've one more party to do yet, eh."
notes: Oyama Taisho: kept as General Oyama for the teasing hail that turns her bulk into a big title.

revision.english: "That's it," came the answer from behind. "You really are an earner!"

"..." Why, whether it would turn into money or not he didn't know, but with her carrying that body along as if to boast of it, he just wanted to boast of something himself, so he had called the place he was off to now a party.
"A stout-built woman, eh," Takami-san said.
"How so — for all that, her husband dotes on her, so there's no standing against her, you know!"

Takami-san was listening in earnest, but he himself knew nothing of the sort in fact. So long as it was a joke that was all he wanted. Thinking this man too was no great talker after all, he changed the subject.
"It's quite hot, isn't it, eh? At this rate will this rainy season be a dry rainy season, eh? That's trouble, eh."
"Why, if it rains the feet coming to the yose will thin out, eh."

"As for customers' feet, I'm seasoned to rubbing little sticks, you know. I've borrowed a bit of another man's ground and I'm growing vegetables. The trouble is that, if the rain doesn't come when it should, they won't do right, eh."
notes: Suri-kogi: I am unsure of the worn-pestle phrase for getting by with few customers, so I have kept it literal and clumsy rather than smoothing it into small audiences.

revision.english: Talking this over as they went, they turned in at the gate of a house. That even here a little patch of cucumbers had been made struck him as genteel.
notes: Okuyukashii taken as genteel, well-bred in the domestic sense, not showy: the small kitchen patch in a gentleman's house pleases his gardener's eye.

revision.english: To get up to the second floor of that house he could only twist his backside up in a queer bobbing way. But when Takami introduced him to the party of six or seven with, "I've brought a rare guest along tonight. I thought we might have him do something for us later. This is the Nekohachi you've heard of," he felt the same pride as always when he cozies up to his customers.
notes: p36 ends mid-sentence on jibun no koto wo, completed by Takami's introduction in p37, so rendered as one paragraph.
Rei no Nekohachi kept as the introducer's flourish: the Nekohachi you've heard of.

revision.english: "This should be fun," somebody cried out.

"That 'the' I took to, eh, I'm a performer with a bit of a name myself, you know. So to come out before great literary gentlemen like yourselves, eh, and not feel stage fright like that, that's lucky for me." Saying this he glanced round the party. Some laughed innocently and none seemed to have taken offence, so he took them for people who would generously take his joke. But to make surer still, meaning to make them understand more, "Only let me tell you beforehand, with rheumatism my body doesn't work like other people's. So if I look to be sitting up stiff like this on purpose, that's why it is, eh, it's not exactly that I'm trembling before you gentlemen."
notes: Kept his eh, you know run-on patter for na and degesu forms, without tidying into respectable grammar. Second sentence is his prepared apology, delivered as part of the act.

revision.english: "ha, ha, ha" came, so he felt safe for a start, and thinking they were his now he shut his mouth for a while.
A study of somebody's novel had begun, but as the subject was actors, he pricked up his ears as a performer in something of the same line.

The man who looked to be the master of the house was someone he had often bathed with in the bathhouse two or three years ago and still met on the road now and then, and he said to Takami-san, "We are just now on 'Tiger.'"
notes: Combined p42-p43 as one English paragraph because p42 ends on a hanging clause leading straight into the quoted speech in p43.

revision.english: "Whose?"
"'Tiger' by Kume. It came out in the May Bunsho Sekai."
notes: Bunsho Sekai kept as roman title as in house style; Kume is the absent author Kume discussed throughout.

revision.english: "I haven't read it," Takami-san answered.
"Few here have read it either — and as the man who went out of his way to put it forward for the June meeting isn't here tonight, I was thinking of letting it pass without a word."

To the question, "What sort of story is it?" the host answered, "I only glanced through it because he asked me by postcard to bring it up — thin if you call it thin, but neatly put together at its low level. The author can hardly have demanded much of himself, so for that author it will do well enough, I suppose — 'Tiger' is the part the hero, a comic actor, has been cast to play. To quote the original, this actor 'had a child already eight years old. And the child had trodden his first stage last year and had before him a future as a shinpa actor like him, no, more proper than him. He thought he would never make the child a comic.'"
notes: Combined p48-p49 as one English paragraph because p48 is a hanging lead into the host's long answer. Kept the summary flat and long-winded as reported talk; kept shinpa unglossed as context supplies a stage child.

revision.english: "..." Hearing this reading, Nekohachi felt he had walked into an awful place. He knew himself that this was a bit of an overblown thought, and yet it sounded just as if they were talking about himself. He had four boys, the eldest fourteen in first year of higher primary, the next twelve in fifth year of elementary, both doing well and both monitors. This twelve year old was good at mimicking his father, and had an art even beyond his father's, but for all that he would not make him a second Nekohachi. No, it was just so as not to let the children see their father mimicking cat fights and animal voices and coaxing good humour out of the customers from up on the koza that he had long ago gone out of his way to choose this inconvenient suburb to live in. Cat turned to tiger, there was no great difference in that.
notes: Kept school years flat as in the source, and kept second Nekohachi as the fixed phrase. Kept koza as in the house voice reference.

revision.english: "The part handed him was just the one part of the tiger." What the host was reading seemed to be the text of the story itself. "Not a man's name. Just the one part dressed up as a real beast of a tiger. He had even taken the byname of animal actor, so what wonder now to be handed the tiger to play. And yet he felt a little sad. Used to it as he long was, profession as he thought it, teasing as he knew it to be, he felt the human inside him being made a fool of, and even felt a little angry. The hero is in that sort of situation."
notes: Kept situation as the English word to leave the loanword joke visible, and kept the paraphrase flat and reported as in the source.

revision.english: "Quite deftly the point the author was aiming at holds together throughout," put in the man with the face like Tenjin-sama, in an earnest tone.
notes: Kept Tenjin-sama as the private nickname per the bible.

revision.english: "..." The English word situation the host had just used stayed in Nekohachi's ears, and he took it to mean something like a painful fix you get caught in. And he himself was in fact fitted into his customers' favour, and had gone and fitted himself right into it, till he was in the state he was in now where he could move neither one way nor the other, so he joked it to himself, quiet. But down underneath he felt the hateful part of the performer's trade all the more.
notes: Kept situation as English to keep the mouthing-English joke visible, and kept fitted/fitted into/fitted part to hold the hame pun that runs into p54. His reading of it as a fix is left as his guess, as in the Japanese.

revision.english: "There is the place where the leader points it out, eh, says that is just Fukai-kun's fitted part," said the priest-like one, close-cropped, with bumps rising fore and aft like a mountain range, the knowing face.

"And then they tell him the whole act will be eaten clean up by Fukai-kun's tiger, and such," the host went on, "and he got that much proud again even. But being the tiger, with no lines to say, there was no call to turn up for rehearsals even. Glad to make use of the day when the child begged to go to Ueno Zoo, he says, well then shall I show you the much talked of hippo, while in truth he means to go and study how a tiger looks. Then on the way, in the tram, he meets a theatre critic, and is asked where he is off to, so he answers, truth to tell, to the zoo to show the child the much talked of hippo, but the sharp critic has him marked, that is a lie, I have heard it already, it is the tiger really."
notes: Kept the retelling flat and a little long-winded as reported talk, without lifting it into a set piece.

revision.english: "There is a kind of sorrow comes out in a bit like that too," said the Tenjin-sama man.
notes: Sorrow renders hiai, first learned here; kept unlyrical to hold for p175/p188. Tenjin-sama kept as nickname per bible.

revision.english: "..." Nekohachi opened his eyes wide as if for the first time on hearing the word sorrow. It seemed to him more and more as if his own affair had been taken and remade and dug into. With his right hand stuck on the tatami and his left laid on the folded hand towel on his knee, admiring at how human feeling falls to the same place whoever feels it, he leaned his head a little back where he sat sideways and said, "I see! To an unlearned one like me a novel seemed a slapdash made-up thing with eight hundred lies strung together in it — though that may have been rude from the start to Sensei gentlemen like yourselves — but to hear it now, sure enough it aims at the true thing, it does, eh"
notes: sorrow renders hiai, kept as in p56; eh and it does for な/でげす tics; em dashes only where the source has ——.

revision.english: "Present-day novels are all like that, of course," the Tenjin-sama man answered, sounding a little angry. "We are different novelists from novelists who write lies and rest satisfied with it!"
notes: Source gives the speaker only as 例のは; taken from the run p56-p61 to be the Tenjin-sama man, who is answered in p59-p61.

revision.english: "Fu, fun," went the knowledge-face man, laughing through his nose.
"How you do flare up," said the very near-sighted-looking man, smiling as he teased him.

"I am not flaring up in particular, only there are plenty of fools in the world who take slapdash popular novels like Hekirurien's or Tokutomi Roka's for the fine standard and pass low, vulgar criticism."
notes: Names left as written, without gloss; this continues the p58 speaker.

revision.english: "Terribly sorry, I am sure," Nekohachi said, keeping a straight face and dipping his head a little, and they all laughed. But this time that alone left him feeling unsatisfied, so he offered up one joke. "I for my part have never yet met a theatre critic in the course of my own researches, no, but once, to study the cry of the earthworm, I squatted up all night in the woods by the Soldiers' Home over there, and they took me for a thief and a detective challenged me, he did, eh."
notes: Kept the long single-sentence patter and the sentence-final appeal for agreement for degesu/na. Soldiers' Home renders haihei-in, the disabled soldiers' home woods; same place as the earthworm story he tells again later. Suika is the Who goes there challenge.

revision.english: "That too, you know, is the result of a kind of sorrow or earnestness," was all the explanation Tenjin-sama gave, and from no one else came any ha, ha, ha.
notes: Kept hiai as sorrow and majime as earnestness flat, and left the thin laughter as ha, ha, ha without upgrading it.

revision.english: ... Nekohachi felt the wind taken clean out of him, against all expectation. And for the first time it struck him that these were not his customers. As an entertainer he might make people cry or laugh, but he had no room left to cry or laugh himself. These people, though, were a cut above even that, for they seemed to study even the feeling of an entertainer himself who makes people cry or laugh and cannot cry or laugh himself. They were specialists in that line, right enough. At this rate an honest humility rose in him to take off his helmet cleanly and own himself beaten, and he asked, "And what did the actor do after that?" What he wanted to know most was about the child. All the same he had quite made up his mind the fall would be that he pleaded the part unworthy and did not go on the stage, or that at least he did not let the child come to the theatre.
notes: Kabuto wo nugu is the idiom for admitting defeat; kept literal as take off his helmet. Ochi kept as fall to hold the rakugo expectation without explaining it.

revision.english: "Just look. You've made a clean confession, haven't you, but if you want to see a tiger you needn't go all the way to the zoo — give anyone a litre or two and he'll turn into one, eh? — Why, shall we go and see that tiger over there? — That won't do. I can't shake this little one off, you see, and he looked back at the child again. There's a passage like that too," the host went on, still with an eye on the book. And everyone forgot Nekohachi and the rest and bent their hearts toward the tiger, but to Nekohachi that tiger was like himself. "For foolishness, Yui's part is much the same. Rather your single tiger part may be the honour, with the popularity gathering on the tiger alone, you know — thinking so I mean to do all I can with all my might, you know — Yes indeed, we for our part are rather counting on your tiger — Much obliged, and Fukai smiled wryly and yet was not a little comforted in his heart."
notes: Kept the host's summary as flat reported talk with the inner jeers left as dash-led run-on, and kept the identification line plain.

revision.english: "That won't do, eh," Nekohachi said, screwing up his face, "to do that situation in a place like that!"
notes: Kept situation as the English loanword he is mouthing; his misuse is left to show.

revision.english: "ufu, fu," a stylish little laugh was heard.
notes: Speaker unattributed in the Japanese, so left unattributed.

revision.english: "Before gentlemen like you, for the likes of me to use cheeky English may have been a mistake —" He had thought better of it that this English might come to what they call compromise, but, "anyhow, if that actor they call Fukai lets the critic's puffing talk away the decent human thought he had managed to hold in that fix, and goes carelessly getting into the swing again, that will be trouble, eh."
notes: Kept compromise as his second guess at situation without smoothing it; the apology and the warning are in his own patter, not in the group's critical terms.

revision.english: "But that is just what makes it interesting, in a way —" the host said.
"But I would never do such a thing," he said, turning earnest as if to show he was not fool enough for that, but neither the host nor any of the rest lent him an ear.
notes: Speech breaks off in the source after sonna koto wa; completed as a full sentence to keep the patter readable.

revision.english: "He went to the zoo and did no more than watch the tiger sitting still and yawning, and yet he came home thinking he had got the tiger's feelings better, somehow, than a handsome lover's feelings. When the first day came and the stuffed tiger came onto the stage and yawned, at that alone there were cries of Fukai, Fukai! from the gallery, and he grew not a little proud. And at the fall of the curtain, when he leapt upon the heroine of the play, gallery first and the whole house with it gave him a great burst of applause."
notes: Kept flat as reported paraphrase; iro-otoko as handsome lover and omuko as gallery without gloss.

revision.english: "Isn't that making fools of people?" It was the words of the much younger man, speaking for the first time.
"That is making a fool of people, right enough," Tenjin-sama put in too, laughing this time.
notes: Kept Tenjin-sama as nickname per bible.

revision.english: A grudge rose in Nekohachi too about the way customers treat him on the kōza, enough to make him want to have his say. "From where I stand, it is the spectators he is making fools of, for getting delighted over trifles, and I daresay he is feeling for the actor himself, eh — spectators are the same as yose customers, you know."
notes: Kept kōza and yose; kept his eh and run-on in place of degesu forms.

revision.english: "Now, about that," Takami-san put in his first question with a mild look, "is it a work where the author is being ironical — I have not read a scrap of it, so I can hardly have an opinion — but to go by what I have just heard?"
"It is irony, to be sure," the knowledge-face man answered in a set-piece tone, "the question is whether the author can be satisfied with irony of so shallow a degree."

"That is it, I suppose." The near-sighted man spoke, for a near-sighted man, with unexpected crispness. "I have not read this one either, but what that lot write is all neatly put together in a small clever way, and without a scrap of background or depth."
notes: Background renders seikatsu-haikei with ruby bakku in the source; the English word is the point here, used straight by the speaker.

revision.english: "Just as Nekohachi-kun said," the knowledge-face man went on, "the author's sympathy for the hero is to be seen, but the way that sympathy is shown is exceedingly thin."

"Thin or not, it is not that it has no background of life." That was the host. "Only, one may say he is an author who can give it no more than a thin background. As for T-kun going out of his way to propose this work, as he is not here tonight his true intent is unclear, but I take it he wanted to make a question for debate of the way it is both put together and yet somehow wanting."
"I daresay that is it."

Nekohachi wanted to make them all laugh by saying he did not know what the hell a back or a haikei was, but as what he had said had been taken up as a point he held his nose high and, with a solemn-looking face, "And so, is this novel finished with that, eh — is there no other fall to it?"
notes: Back keeps bakku as sound and haikei keeps haikei as sound, against background elsewhere, because here Nekohachi hears both as noise. Fall renders ochi, his rakugo word for a punchline, which he misapplies to a novel.

revision.english: ha, ha, ha! Only two or three of them just laughed.
To Nekohachi it felt like the roar had come at a strange place.

"You're no rakugo man," Tenjin-sama had stuck in another unasked word, or so it felt to Nekohachi, but he saw at once his own ignorance was being teased, so he buried his awkwardness in another apology.
"Yes, quite sorry about that."

"There is no ochi, no fall, in a novel, but what Nekohachi would take for a fall is what closes this story, and it is that which keeps the piece, thin as it is, alive. Fukai gets his great applause at the curtain and is going off proud in his sewn-up shape when from the shadow of the dark flats something cries 'Father' and clings to him. He looks back in surprise and finds his own child crying, child as he is, at the foolish part his father has played. He too cannot help crying, now at last. And then, 'the tiger and the human child wept together for a while in the shadow of the dark background,' that is how it ends."
notes: Kept ochi with gloss as fall, since the joke is his asking a novel for a rakugo punchline. Kept the paraphrase flat and long-winded on purpose, and kept background for haikei to hold the network with the group's critical word.

revision.english: "The last bit has a good swing to it, eh," the near-sighted man said to them all.
notes: Unsure of futteru here: I take it as stage slang for having flair or lift, and render it flat rather than upgrading to brilliant or moving.

revision.english: "That without it the whole piece goes slack shows," the knowledge-face man put in, "how feeble a thing this story is, don't you think?"
"That's it, eh," the host answered as if the strength had gone out of his shoulders. "In the end it isn't much of a piece."

"..." Nekohachi stared with his eyes opened wide, as if thunderstruck, when he came to hear of this last business of weeping together. He knew well enough himself that this too was a face put on and exaggerated on purpose, and yet at the same time, before he knew it, what was always kept hidden in the bottom of his heart seemed to have come out upon his face, for the grief over his own trade and the wavering over whether to make his second son into a second Nekohachi had been coaxed out together at once. He tried not to show people a face so ill-suited to his comic trade, but the harder he tried the less the face itself would obey him, quite the other way, and if he saw it in a mirror he thought it must look like a blubbering face. But without patching it up any more, plainly, "Well, I am impressed," he showed his respect as if the story were the very work of the company present. "I've got the same sort of sorrow myself, and it truly struck home, it did, eh. But if I too may be allowed the one, what you gentlemen would call a criticism, this Fukai playing a part against his own wish and letting his child see it, that I think was a grave mistake, eh?"
notes: Kept 'sorrow' for 悲哀 and 'second Nekohachi' as fixed phrasing per bible; kept the self-known exaggeration and blubbering face straight, without ennobling into insight.

revision.english: "That's neither here nor there, it's no question for the author."
notes: Speaker unattributed in source; left unattributed. From p93 it answers as the Tenjin-like man's opinion.

revision.english: "But with me it won't do to let it go at that," he said, hitching himself forward a little on his knees as if he were well and truly joining the debate now, standing up to the Tenjin-sama man. "I've got children myself, you see, my eldest and my second boy go to grade school, and the second, the twelve-year-old, when it comes to copying me he's a genius, so if I'm out sick from my seat he says he'll go in Dad's place, eh"
notes: Son's line is indirect in the Japanese; kept as quoted offer in Dad's voice.

revision.english: "Ha, ha," the Tenjin-sama man laughed, in a laugh half as if impressed and half as if making fun.

"Trade it may be, but with the old man already doing fool tricks, I don't want the child laughed at too, so to keep the children from coming near the yose where their dad appears I've gone out of my way to live in this awkward suburb on purpose, eh"
notes: He calls himself oya ji here, not father; kept as old man and dad to hold the shift.

revision.english: "Something of that sort of feeling does come out in it, too," the host answered him, "but that is not all the story is about, so this is fine as it is, I suppose."
"Don't you despise your own art too much, Nekohachi-kun?" the near-sighted man put the question to him like that.
"Of course," he stuck for a moment, but there was no need to think it over. "There's nothing else for it, eh. Human as I am, such as I am, I've got to make even a tiger's cry to eat my rice, eh"
"But," the other went on, "unlike you, the hero of this piece always takes his child along to the theatre so he can become a performer all the sooner, doesn't he?"
notes: Speaker unnamed in the Japanese; taken to be the near-sighted man continuing from p97.

revision.english: "There's plenty of fathers like that about, and that's the trouble." Nekohachi was none too pleased. A performer is human too, and yet there seemed to be no sympathy for him in this company. Hanging about in a place like this he would likely not get so much as a penny by way of thanks, he thought, and inwardly chanted Tō Enmei's "let me go home, come—come, let me go home." That set him straight. And as the night deepened outside the open second floor, along with his children what worried him most again was the seedlings in his plot.
notes: Kept Tō Enmei as inward chant for wanting to leave, literal rather than literary; kept children, fee-thanks and seedlings as repeated network words.

revision.english: Then came, "What sticks in my craw more than any of that," and he wanted to say here was the Tenjin-sama fellow off on his chatter again, only it kept the same earnest tone as ever, "is this author's flippant attitude. An anonymous monthly review in the Jiji Shinpō abused this piece roundly, saying Kume must be a hopeless fellow to rest satisfied with anything so shallow, so I read it myself in earnest to see how shallow a thing it could be, and to me it did not seem anything to sneer at. But when I asked our host here tonight, it seems that reviewer is Kume himself."
notes: Joined p102 lead-in with p103 speech as one English paragraph; kept Tenjin-sama nickname and Jiji Shinpō unexplained as in source.

revision.english: "Yes," Nekohachi meant to put in unwillingly enough, but without knowing it he was grinning. And just as he had thought, he took it that with this author the fall or conclusion of the piece had not come from his true intent, his real intent was to fool people. And he took to this Kume fellow all at once. "Isn't he a bit of a witty soul, like Sanba of old, eh?"
notes: Kept ochi as fall to leave his rakugo expectation visible; kept Sanba as bare name without gloss.

revision.english: "He's not so flippant as all that, Kume as an author, eh," said the knowledge-face fellow.
"You can tell that from his work up till now, can't you?" That was the near-sighted man.
"If he's a flippant man, it's only natural he makes flippant work. Whether to like it or dislike it is left to the reader's side."
notes: No speaker named in the text; taken as the host, as p108 has Nekohachi receive it as the host's argument.

revision.english: "So it's up to the customer, is it, eh," Nekohachi took the host's argument this way. And growing eager to cozy up to it, "But he's a man with a deal of teasing wit in him, and I think him a great man, eh?"
notes: Tea-wit for 茶気, his performer’s word for love of a droll trick; kept as teasing rather than ennobled.

revision.english: "There's great and great, you know."
"Wa-ha, ha," two or three of them raised their voices together.

"Sensei," the student-like fellow who had not said a word till now spoke for the first time, his words carrying that nervous tone. "I've not read a thing of Mr Kume's, so I've no right to say anything about the man, but it seems to me a piece of fiction has no depth unless the author's personality is backing it, eh?"
notes: Sensei kept; addressed to the room, presumably the host. Personality backing for 人物が裏づけ.

revision.english: "You always talk like an idealist, but even the realists on the other side would never deny that."
"Then I feel easy about that, but..."
"Only we don't come to a stop at the sort of thing you mean."
"That's just what I can't..." the other said, cocking his head a little to one side.
"Even if the man's character comes out, unless a life of that character comes out with it, it still won't be concrete, will it?"
notes: Character for 人格 and concrete for ぐたい的, keeping the group's borrowed abstraction flat against Nekohachi's patter.

revision.english: "..." The nervous student smiled now and made his bow. "Then even I can understand that."

"..." He wanted to say, I haven't the least idea what any of it is about, eh. What they call realism he didn't understand, and gutai and kuutai and that he didn't understand either, so he only thought of that konnyaku question-and-answer of the rakugo man.
notes: Left genjitsu-shugi as realism and gutai/kuutai as sound kept in roman, to match concrete in p116 and to leave his non-understanding visible; left konnyaku question-and-answer unglossed per style.

revision.english: In the meantime two or three more novels seemed to come up for discussion, but they did not take his interest the way the tiger had, so with his eyes on the Western picture he could make nothing of hanging on the wall to the right of where he sat and on the gilt lettering of the books in the bookcase knocked together out of beer crates to his front left, he bit back the yawns that kept coming. The host did say, We had better give Nekohachi some sake, but, "No, I am more for the katsubushi side," he answered, and had mochi cakes brought out by the host's wife. And as he talked with her about the pleasure of growing vegetables and about the bringing up of each other's children, he got two or three magazines the children looked likely to read.
notes: Joined p119-p120 as one English sentence group since p119 ends mid-clause on keredomo; kept katsubushi literally though unsure whether snack, side dish, or set phrase for declining drink, rather than smoothing to sweets.

revision.english: Then from Takami-san, "Well, let us have you do something, eh."

"..." Now this from here on was at last his own world, he thought, and the damp feeling he had got from the tiger story went off somewhere, and he wanted them to think better of his art than of the tiger. He had righted himself before he knew it, and in his readiness there was the same braced spirit as on the kouza, and before he had yet done anything he could hear his own mimic voice. He bent the little finger of his right hand like a hook and started to carry it to his just opened mouth, then stopped and looked the finger over, half to himself, "Sweaty and short of oil, I wonder if it will go, eh."
After wiping the sweat off the finger once with his hand-towel, he kept his face to tell nothing of where it would come from, and went hohokekyo.
notes: The face that tells nothing of where the wind blows is his performer's blank before the cry; I have kept it as work, not weather.

revision.english: "A fine thing, eh," Tenjin-sama blurted straight out in praise, but that jarred.

"That just now was the nightingale in its cage, now the valley-crossing —" kekyo, kekyo, kekyo, hohokekyo! Then straight on the voices of the pine cricket, the bell cricket, the kutsuwamushi. Then crow, skylark, quail. With his joined lips pushed flat out to the front, the voice of the mole-cricket. Saying it might be a bother to the neighbours quieted to sleep by now, the male crane and the female crane told apart in the cry. The grass lark's voice too he let them hear.
notes: I have left the insect and bird names as a list and kept kutsuwamushi in roman, as the catalogue is load-bearing.

revision.english: To every cry, every cry, the listeners being listeners he could go all out, and they all seemed to be listening quietly, and it went as he wished and he was satisfied, and meaning for a bonus to show them the voice of the earthworm, "What they generally call an earthworm crying, that they say is the voice of the mole-cricket, but the earthworm cries too, eh," with that for a preface giving again a voice something like the mole-cricket, "If with this you do their voice you will see. For that study I once sat up all night in the wood at the Haiheiin, but when footsteps sound, their voice breaks off for a while. I crouch there and wait a bit and then try it again, and if our voice is exactly like theirs, they answer straight off, and if it is wrong, there is no reply."
notes: p127 breaks off into the speech in p128, so I have kept them as one paragraph in English. The doubling of cry upon cry is in the source and I have kept it as repetition, not varied away.

revision.english: "ha, ha, ha!" The host let out a specially loud laugh.
"It's the truth, you know," he pleaded his seriousness. About the 'reply' — that was just his usual joke slipping out.
notes: His 'reply' is his own joking word for the worm answering back; I was unsure whether to gloss it, and have left it as he says it.

revision.english: "Well, abroad there are men who have gone at it on a larger scale and have even studied the language of monkeys."
notes: Speaker is not named in the text; reads as the host carrying on from his loud laugh at p129.

revision.english: "If I ever get to learn English or something, I will try it myself, eh —"
"But monkeys do not use English."
notes: Speaker is not named in the text;reads as one of the group capping Nekohachi rather than the host.

revision.english: "Wa ha, ha," two or three of them came out together.

"..." He felt quite as if his own stock in trade had been taken from him, and his spirits fell a little flat. Just to cover it, "They say on learned grounds that the monkey has turned into man, but in the story here the tiger has turned into a monkey, eh."
notes: o-kabu wo torareta is his patter for having his thunder stolen; kept as stock in trade to hold the yose sense.

revision.english: "No, we are glad to have it in your animal mimicry too," the host answered.

"That aside," the man with the face like Tenjin-sama, whom he had till now thought a disagreeable fellow, asked him a good question this time. "I want to hear your motive for coming to do such things, eh."
notes: Kept Tenjin-sama as in the bible; the ne is the man's, not Nekohachi's na.

revision.english: "Motive, you say —?"
"Well, call it the first notion that started it."

"I see, eh — for all you see of me I wasn't a farmer from the first, no, nor any born artiste neither, though I daresay that goes for any of us, eh," he joked, and then he told of old days that held memories even for him. After one arm and one leg had gone useless he had talked it over with his wife and turned candy-seller. But just blowing the Chinese flute and hobbling along, hobbling along, not the snottiest-nosed brat would buy from him. The first day was clean nothing, clean zero, and on the second day at last he sold ten sen's worth. He left that one silver coin with the child to please him with it, and child being child, he set it down on the bridge rail and went off to play, and in between another child took it. On the third day too he went out for trade because he went, but this was never going to do, he gave up hope, and stretched his legs out on the Yoshiwara embankment and sat there in a daze, thinking. "It was here I got a heaven-sent idea, and got in me the makings of the performer I would be one day, eh," and having got a small laugh from his hearers with that, he moved on to how he learned the cry of the frogs. "Before I knew it, any number of frogs were crying out in the paddies." As now, he showed how he had turned his eyes that way then, stuck his face a little sideways, and a good deal handier than when he had tried it that time, closing his hand as if round an egg and bringing his mouth to the hole at the top, he let out a little kuk kuk of a cry. "When I tried it myself, out of all those many frogs just six or seven turned round my way. I thought that strange and wondered a while, and then once more," he said, changing to a kak kak of a voice to show them, "when I tried it, this time all the frogs except those six or seven turned to face me, every one of them."
notes: Kept Don-geinin as 'any born artiste neither' for the self-deprecating joke; unsure of exact nuance of Don beyond born or proper performer, left as modest denial.
Kept Chinese flute for toujin-bue as candy-seller's flute without gloss, and Yoshiwara embankment as place-name the passage gives.
Kept frog cries as kuk kuk / kak kak to read as act rather than nature writing; hand-as-egg description follows the Japanese closely and may still be clumsy.

revision.english: The truth was, he did not suppose it had gone quite so cleanly as all that, but there was no witness who had stood by and seen it at the time, so with an easy mind he made the story pretty. "And what I found was, the first way of crying was the females, and the one after was the males. And there were only six or seven males there, and all the rest were females."
notes: Kept male/female for osu/mesu to leave the frogs as frogs; the tidying is admitted in the narration, so left it visible.

revision.english: "Interesting!"
notes: Speaker not named; took it as the Tenjin-sama, as p144 names his praise.

revision.english: "..." He had had the Tenjin-sama's praise, and his own delight welled up still more. "This was my first notion, eh," and then when he went to where the children gathered and showed them the mimicry, the candy sold better than you would think. And from the next day the frog candy-man was waited for wherever he went.
"Sensei, candy is quite a paying thing, eh, with only five sen laid out it came to thirty sen, forty sen at the time."
"What made you give up such a good paying line, then?"
notes: Speaker not named; took it as the same questioner continuing the motive talk from p138.

revision.english: "Why, my hobby got too much for me, eh. Shall I say mimicking the cry of things was in me by nature? I mimic anything. No, whatever cries, if I cannot mimic it I study it till I can. Among my customers there are often orders like cry the firefly or cry the colic-worm, but that not even a genius beyond me could likely do. As for me, nowadays cats fighting and the cries of insects and birds have got common, and I cannot keep up unless I mimic aeroplanes and motorcars too."
notes: Kept cry for hotaru and senki no mushi as orders, and kept the animal list flat as catalogue, not nature writing.

revision.english: "Why, there is carelessness in mimicry too," the host said, "and by that carelessness many things get vulgarised."

"At that rate you will only throw yourself away and go downhill, won't you? Rather than that, why not talk just as you told your own history now, natural and without frills, even when you go to the yose. Wouldn't that be a good deal more natural and interesting?" said the Tenjin-sama-like man again.
"I think that would be good too," the near-sighted man agreed.
"But my life is in making fools of the customers from up on the kouza and showing it, that is where it is."
"That's right, eh," said Takami-san, with his arms round both his knees, as if taking my side. "His offhand sarcasm and heckling when they come, why, they are a treat to hear."

"In return, when I get to a certain point, I make my compromise and my concession, eh. There are times I even cry the firefly and the colic-worm for them. They are things that do not cry in any case, so it does not matter how I do it, see," and then putting on a sharp look, "You don't understand much yourself, eh, can a colic-worm cry? If that will not do for you, I have taken your wooden gate charge already, so you can get home quick — only that would be too bare, so at the end I let the other fellow save face too — but you don't want to go home halfway either. Truth is, I don't want to go home either — that is what I make of it."
notes: Quoted heckle shifts from watakushi to oira and omeesan, rough downtown address: kept as plain you and I with blunter syntax, no dialect spelling.
Wooden gate charge for kidaisen, compromise for dakyo, as fixed through-page terms.

revision.english: "I wonder if that is a kind of ochi too?" asked the near-sighted man, laughing.
notes: Kept ochi for his rakugo punchline word, as before.

revision.english: "That, I take it, is a kind of conclusion, eh." This was Nekohachi trying to take back what he felt he had fumbled a little earlier over the ending of the Tiger. "But then, when I get called to the princes and the like, why, gyagya-gya," and with that baring his teeth, goggling his eyes, screwing his face into something queer, he showed them cats at it fighting, and set them all off at once. But keeping a straight face himself, he went on, "It is not barnyard fowl, showing you cats kicking at each other is still hardly out of place. When the person before me is a lady, I can well hear the laugh from behind the fan where she hides her noble face. But at times, when I went up to Mr ___ for instance, I was told, they say you are good not only at mimicry but at rakugo too, let our guests hear something funny, so I declined. It is far too awesome for me, I cannot. But I was pressed, so perform a turn I did, perform one I did, and it is a strange thing, from the very start not a bit of it gets across. As we only know our own low-down society, of course the story falls there too. 'Oi, Hachi, are you there,' says I," and with that he showed hitching his backside and sitting on the step at the entrance, "from the first that does not get across what it is about, 'beranmei, bare-arsed you cannot hitch up, eh,' none of that ready wit gets across. Begging pardon for a rude thing to say, there is nothing to bite on, where there ought to come a roar they all sit prim."
notes: I kept the blanks as Mr ___: the source writes OOO-sama, discretion performed in the telling, so I did not fill it.
Hachi is left as Hachi: the rakugo stock butt the bible flags at p155, quoted inside Nekohachi's failed upstairs turn.
gyagya-gya and the beranmei hitch-up line are kept as act, not smoothed into description: the joke about a bare backside that cannot hitch itself up is meant to fall flat upstairs.

revision.english: "It's because the way you live is clean different, you know."
notes: Speaker unattributed in the source; taken as one of the gentlemen answering Nekohachi, left unattributed as in the Japanese.

revision.english: "That would be it, eh." He thought these learned gents were different after all. What he had run up against himself in the flesh and still could not explain, they had made clear for him in a single word. Truly the life of the upper folk and the life of the likes of us is clean different. The way we live is as far apart as the moon and a soft-shell turtle.
notes: Moon and soft-shell turtle renders the set phrase for things incomparable; kept literal rather than smoothing to worlds apart.

revision.english: Thinking so, he had the back row-houses in mind. First the blacksmith, slow to get going, always getting shouted at by his mountain-goddess. Next the woman hairdresser, no telling how many men she has gone through. Next to her our own place, and next to that the tram conductor, clattering about while folk are still sound asleep and off out to his bell-ringing trade. And right at the dead end the blear-eyed lame clam-seller. In summer they are a near stark-naked society, but of the lot only our place is anything like human. The field work is only my spare-time work, but even so there is an ease there those gaunt craze-driven lot know nothing of. And the daikon and leaf greens I give away free to them at times. For all that we are rattling Edokko who keep no overnight money, I born from a geisha's belly in a famous Asakusa restaurant, my wife first-bathed in Kanda upper water. And with that he wanted to show off a bit of what he knew before them all.
notes: Mountain-goddess is his joking word for the blacksmith's wife, kept literal.
I am unsure who the gaunt craze-driven lot are meant to be in this slide, the great-house folk just spoken of or the hungry upper world at large; left vague as in the source rather than naming them.

revision.english: There was a time a grand carriage stopped at the mouth of our row, you see. They must have known well enough how poor we lived, but, "Is this the house of the performer called Nekohachi?" "Yes," and I was a bit put to it by that. "Then is the master himself at home?" "Yes, the master has just gone to the bath and is out," hardly could I step out as the man himself in nothing but a loincloth, eh. "If you will wait a moment, I will go and call him directly," I said, and stepped outside for the moment. I gave my wife a wink, but she made an awkward face. I made as if to leave the house and slipped straight into the blacksmith's by the entrance, told his wife the story and got her to bring a kimono and sash, and putting on the look of a man just back from the bath, with a borrowed towel wetted with water and a soap box in hand, "Sorry to have kept you waiting, I am Nekohachi, what is your business?" Pupil and master with faces not a bit different, no wonder they found it strange. "In fact I have come from the ___ house, and just now your name came up there, and as you are said to do an amusing act you are to come at once, so I was told to come and fetch you," that is what he said.
notes: Kept the blank in ○○家 as the ___ house as in the source, per bible, rather than filling or smoothing it.
Read the unattributed questions as the messenger's and the answers as Nekohachi first as the supposed pupil, then as the master himself.

revision.english: Just then the near-sighted man said he would be in a fix if it got any later, and stood up. He looked up sidelong at that profile to show a touch of displeasure, but the man never noticed. And on top of that two others stood up too, and went home together with him. If this were the yose, with the wooden gate charge already settled, it would be easier to give it up. But when a man has at last settled his heart and keeps on speaking straight, to walk out on him in the middle struck him as the true walk-out, and he could not give it up. He wanted to tell them he would come out and haunt them from some dark alley on the way, but with the host among them there were eager listeners still left, so the thread of his talk was hardly broken.
notes: Kept 'wooden gate charge' for 木戸銭 and 'give it up' twice for 諦め to hold the repetition. Kept 'walk-out' for 失敬 to hold the pun on leaving and rudeness, and 'haunt' for 化けてでてやる to hold the monster network from p6.

revision.english: "To come and fetch me at once just because my name happened to come up in talk, that is just like the nobility, eh. Even then, it is not that I will not go, you see, but with an Edokko temper, when they start with money straight off, I get contrary, eh."
"But if it is business, there is no need for that, is there?" the host objected.

"No, business or no business, when they come at me squarely with how much will you come for, well, damn it, do as you please, is how I feel, eh. If it is a contribution then a contribution will do, and if they can pay then let them quietly pay what befits their station."
notes: Kept 'contribution' for 寄附 and 'money / how much / pay' blunt, per the fee network, without tidying his run-on patter.

revision.english: "That old-fashioned stuff will never do. Better to ask beforehand, no coming unless it is so many yen and more, and an aristocrat, as an aristocrat, to pay far higher than a commoner, that nowadays is rather the sensible way."
"But when money is named it turns dirty, eh."
"That's the old stale smell about performers today!"
notes: Speaker unattributed in the source; carried as the host's cut-in from p163-p165.

revision.english: "Performers today can't do any new tricks anyway, eh. If they don't come out to fetch you proper, why, I mostly turn them right down flat, eh. One time there I was, naked, lugging a hoe out in my plot, when a messenger from Viscount ___ came all the way to the field, and it got settled for such a day, from such an hour, but when he asks me how much will it take, I broke it off outright. A performer lives on spirit, eh, but then, if the fancy takes me, I'll go for nothing."
notes: Kept the blank as Viscount ___ per bible; naked with a hoe kept flat as inventory, not euphemised.

revision.english: "That may not be a bad thing either, but then, what has become of this pig-farming Takami-kun means to start," so saying, the host turned the talk aside. And as if he knew quite well about things wholly apart from novels, talk that way went on a while among them all.

"Just because I am here, no need to talk of nothing but animals, eh," he got the joke said, but he was already pretty well worn out. Likely because he had still not taken the supper he should take, and hunger was coming on.

The other guests were trading easy talk like how the trams had stopped anyway, but he wished they would all go home soon. And as his spirits sank, what strangely kept on his mind was the fee for tonight, if none comes then none will do, but whether it would come from Takami-san, or from the master here, or whether it would end just like this. Plenty here to chatter along with a professional like himself, but none that looked likely to have sense as listeners.
notes: Fee kept blunt for谢礼; dashes in the source rendered by commas to keep the fretting run-on without adding em dashes.

revision.english: He bore it, thinking it would be clear when this meeting broke up, which would be any moment now. But starting with Takami-san, no one considerately made a move, and to go dully home ahead of the rest would be dull too, so he took the host's wife again for company and talked of his own plot, what till now he had left forgotten. It was nothing he made trade of, particularly, but when talk turned to the plot, whoever he had for his listener, he at times grew so keen he forgot himself, and the spirit came back into him. This, as he had long thought, was his own taste, his pleasure. So,
notes: Okusan taken as the host's wife, the garden-and-children talk partner from p119-p120, not his own wife; rendered as 'the host's wife' to keep the cast clear. Kept the trailing 'So,' to carry the dangling de into the speech in p173.

revision.english: "Eggplants, cucumbers, they'll be coming ready from here on, so whenever you have need I'll give you some," he said, covering over his own disagreeable face that would keep turning sullen. And the hand he had till now held back a little he put out three times running to the mochi cakes.

It was close on one in the morning, when the cranes crying over at the veterans' hospital came through clear, and everyone got to their feet. He got to his feet too, brisk on purpose, and went down the stairs with the rest, but with the old magazines and the leftover cakes and senbei stuffed in his breast, if that was to take the place of tonight's thanks, it felt silly, and here in secret he wanted to hold that tiger close and cry a while somehow. It was not that he was fretting because he had got no money, that much he knew from the point of being an Edokko — and that too you would know if you saw how his wife, an Edokko herself, gave in to a woman's weak heart and now and then tried to keep overnight money, and he knocked her about till she spent it all — but set beside a farmer's working life, this body of his that had to show people worthless tricks to live on felt sad somehow, all over again.
notes: Veterans' hospital for Haiheiin: the disabled soldiers' home whose wood was his earthworm ground. Overnight money kept as the fixed phrase for yoigoshi no kane. Wife-beating kept blunt as in the text.

revision.english: "It's only a little, you know—" Takami-san, who was not without thought for others, slipped him two yen coins in secret once they were outside, so he could pull himself together a little. And perhaps for that reason he could pay the more respect even to the host who came along behind saying to them all, "I'll see you partway, for a walk." But for himself — perhaps out of a nasty habit — what a stingy spirit, he thought himself mean. And if he could have it, he wanted to quit being a performer from tomorrow.
notes: Two paragraphs made one in English because one sentence runs across the break from ato kara tsuite kite to the host's offer. En-suke two pieces taken as two one-yen coins. Self-contempt kept flat, without explaining it away.

revision.english: By now the only thing on his mind was the weather. Wondering when the rain would ever come, he looked up at the sky and hobbled along behind them all, hop hop, pitched to be heard by whoever he could not make out in the dim road,
"Tiger—monkey—pig, tonight it has been nothing but animal talk, eh."
"And your frogs besides," came the answer, and it was the knowledge-face man.

Thinking suddenly of the nervous one from the konnyaku question and answer, he could hear voices chatting away ahead with the Tenjin-sama fellow. Presently they passed the woods of the Invalids Home, and in another step or two was the mouth of his own row house alley.
notes: I took the voices ahead to be the nervous student-like man talking with the Tenjin-like man, but the subject is left vague so I kept it vague. I kept konnyaku question and answer literal rather than explaining the joke.

revision.english: "This back in here is where I live, it is a squalid hole, but if you are ever passing please step in," he said, taking his leave of them all. But he had one thing left he wanted to say, so he took one step forward and added, "And my plot, if you peep past the trifoliate orange hedge just there you will see it. It is dark now so you will not see well, but eggplants and cucumbers will be coming on plenty from now, more than the family alone can ever eat,"
notes: Kikokugaki is the trifoliate orange hedge around his plot. I kept it as a plain plant name without gloss.
Kept as silence in the text: no answer comes to the vegetable offer.

revision.english: "Well, gentlemen, I will take my leave here."

The row house folk, who seemed already to be waiting even now for the eggplants and cucumbers to come, were all fast asleep. And the only one to greet this Edoya Nekohachi on his way home was the dog kept by the neighbourhood sake shop. But even to himself it seemed rare to be feeling so humble, and so human, as tonight.
notes: Edoya Nekohachi is his full house name, claimed here on the way home. I kept it unvaried rather than smoothing it to Nekohachi.

revision.english: The wooded road by the Disabled Veterans' Hospital was so dark that, for the sake of passers turning in from the tram street, he had petitioned some time ago to be allowed to put up a gas lamp with his own name written in it, for his own advertisement. The permission looked as if it would be hard to get, but that no longer mattered to him now. It only came to this, that nobody would needlessly give himself a stomach-ache over it.
notes: I kept the petition flat as inventory, not as ambition. The last sentence is uncertain: I read it as his gnomic shrug that no one frets himself for nothing, and left the belly-ache wording visible rather than smoothing it.

revision.english: It did nag at him, after a fashion, that he had taken this overnight money with his stingy spirit, but whatever he might buy for them the children would surely be fast asleep by now. The toy shops and the food shops along the tram street would surely have their shutters closed too. So he would likely laugh it off as having got, the other way round, what he himself ought to have paid out in school fees.
notes: Overnight money keeps the earlier wording for the two yen coins. I took monthly school fees to mean what he pays out for his sons, received contrary-wise tonight, and had to decide this anyway.

revision.english: In any case, resolved to tell his wife at once the story from tonight's novel, and to make her taste it just as he had fully felt there an entertainer's sorrow, he drew near to the door of his own house.
notes: Sorrow keeps hiai unvaried. I kept make her taste it straight, without softening it into sharing or teaching.

revision.english: "Terribly sorry, I am sure," Nekohachi said, keeping a straight face and dipping his head a little, and they all laughed. But this time that alone left him feeling unsatisfied, so he offered up one joke. "I for my part have never yet met a theatre critic in the course of my own researches, no, but once, to study the cry of the earthworm, I squatted up all night in the woods by the Veterans' Home over there, and they took me for a thief and a detective challenged me, he did, eh."

To every cry, every cry, the listeners being listeners he could go all out, and they all seemed to be listening quietly, and it went as he wished and he was satisfied, and meaning for a bonus to show them the voice of the earthworm, "What they generally call an earthworm crying, that they say is the voice of the mole-cricket, but the earthworm cries too, eh," with that for a preface giving again a voice something like the mole-cricket, "If with this you do their voice you will see. For that study I once sat up all night in the wood at the Veterans' Home, but when footsteps sound, their voice breaks off for a while. I crouch there and wait a bit and then try it again, and if our voice is exactly like theirs, they answer straight off, and if it is wrong, there is no reply."

It was close on one in the morning, when the cranes crying over at the Veterans' Home came through clear, and everyone got to their feet. fork.question: Do the two readings name the same crux in different words, or different cruxes — Nekohachi's associative performed consciousness as the form to preserve, versus the unblended collision of his tongue with the literati's and the unresolved tiger-mirror as the structure to preserve? They share patter and 'The Tiger', but each makes central what the other leaves secondary, and adopting one will direct choices the other would direct differently, so the text does not settle it as mere rewording.

options.author: first-read (Wonder)
options.case:
- keep Nekohachi's patter as work, not local colour His banter on the tram in p2-p10 is not decoration before the serious part begins; it is the act itself, carried on in public because passengers have become an audience and a comeback is professionally compulsory. Again at the meeting he tests jokes, misapplies the borrowed word "situation" (p67-p69), apologises, recovers, and feels the flatness when は、は、は does not come (p63). If English tidies this into witty repartee it ennobles him; if it renders it as broad dialect comedy it does to him exactly what his audiences do. For the English: he must never become quaint Cockney or stage-Japanese. Use dropped, run-on, self-interrupting colloquial syntax, repetitions and verbal tics in place of the sentence-ending な and the self-deprecating でげす forms, and let the dignity show through competence and generosity, not through making his grammar more respectable.
- keep the ramble, because the ramble is the consciousness The narration stays glued to Nekohachi's mind, and that mind does not proceed: on the tram it slides from a heckle to why a comedian must not laugh, to protecting a voice he does not drink for, to caterpillars in a ditch and cutworms that, like thieves and like himself, work only at night (p10-p14). The garden returns at every pressure point (p20, p31-p33, p100, p158, p172-p173) and is still what he offers the departing gentlemen at his own gate (p182). A fluent version that breaks this into themed paragraphs, or clarifies the transitions, has rationalised away the man. For the English: do not iron out the long, associative sentences in which cabbages, a bath, a fee and a son succeed one another, and do not cut the lists. Keep the repetitions - animals, vegetables, children, money - as repetitions: they are Berman's networks, the web the story is made of, not redundancy to be varied away.
- let 'The Tiger' stay a clumsy paraphrase, not a set piece Half the story is a second-hand retelling of Kume's tale of a comic actor cast as a tiger whose child finds him weeping in the wings (p48-p90). It would be easy to polish this into a moving story-within-the-story. In the text it arrives as reported talk, interrupted, jargon-dusted (シチュエイション, バック), and judged thin by everyone present. Its power for Nekohachi is precisely that this mediocre fiction has got his life: four sons, a gifted twelve-year-old he has moved to the suburbs to keep away from the yose (p50, p93-p95). Prettify the paraphrase and his response looks disproportionate; sentimentalise his response and the literati's cool verdict loses its sting. For the English: keep the embedded summary flat and a little long-winded, keep its pathos unlyrical, and keep Nekohachi's interventions in his own terms (a father should not let the child see it) rather than translating them into the group's critical vocabulary. Let the reader feel the identification before Nekohachi names 悲哀 for himself.
options.tradeoff: Protects Nekohachi's associative consciousness and professional patter, at the risk of under-stating the structural clash with the literati and the ending's undecidability.

options.author: crux-check (Wonder)
options.case:
- The collision of languages is the action: close third-person narration saturated with Nekohachi's Edokko yose patter (でげす, な, self-deprecating jokes, internal 洒落 he performs even to himself) set against the literati's imported jargon (シチュエイション, バック, 現実主義/具体) that he literally cannot parse. He is never off stage—he swallows '小奈良の小大仏' (p8), turns a tram ride into a 高座 (p5-9), negotiates every humiliation as a gag—while they study that very compulsion as '悲哀' in Kume's '虎'. Strip the register gap and the plot (a mimic taken to a research society) has no tension left: his mishearings of 'situation' as a predicament he is trapped in (p53), his gratitude at being quoted back as criticism (p79-82), and his final triumph in performance (p124-136) all only register because we hear him thinking and speaking in a different tongue from theirs. For the English: Keep two audible Englishes unblended: Nekohachi in a working, comic, self-interrupting stage patter full of swallowed retorts and asides, the writers in flat, borrowed critical abstraction; never polish either into the same literary fluency, and let the reader feel when neither fully understands the other.
- The mirrored tiger must stay unresolved: Nekohachi condemns Fukai for letting his child see the debasing role (p91-95) and has moved to the suburbs to hide his own, yet eagerly performs, fishes for praise and a fee (p171-177), and misreads Kume's anonymous self-denunciation as proof Kume is a wit after his own heart (p103-110). The text itself flags that even his grief-stricken face is partly exaggeration he half-knows about (p91), and ends not in renunciation—he plans to retell the novel to his wife (p188)—but in a 'rare' humble, human feeling (p185) alongside gas-lamp advertising and the night's two coins. If the translation settles him as either dignified artist-victim (the literati's '悲哀' made true) or comic butt the reader pities from above, it picks the side the story refuses: his sorrow is real and performed at once, his pride in hiding the act from his sons coexists with delight that '例の猫八' is known (p37-39), and that undecidability is what the whole mirrored structure was built to produce. For the English: Hold the double exposure in the English: render his self-recognitions and the closing humility straight, without irony markers, ennoblement, or a softened/resolved ending, so the reader—not the prose—decides how much is insight and how much is act.
options.tradeoff: Protects the register collision and the unresolved sorrow/performance double exposure, at the risk of under-stating the ramble and repetitious networks as the substance of Nekohachi's consciousness.

fork.head_reason: They name different things, not the same thing in different words: Option 0 makes the crux the preservation of Nekohachi's rambling, repetitious, professionally performed consciousness and the deliberate flatness of the embedded paraphrase, while Option 1 makes it the unblended clash of his English with the literati's and the refusal to resolve sorrow against performance. Because that difference will recur in register, paragraphing, the retelling and the ending, and being wrong about which governs would be expensive, this goes up as a fork.

Again at the meeting he tests jokes, misapplies the borrowed word "situation" (p67-p69), apologises, recovers, and feels the flatness when は、は、は does not come (p63). If English tidies this into witty repartee it ennobles him; if it renders it as broad dialect comedy it does to him exactly what his audiences do.

crux.for_the_english: do not iron out the long, associative sentences in which cabbages, a bath, a fee and a son succeed one another, and do not cut the lists. Keep the repetitions - animals, vegetables, children, money - as repetitions: they are Berman's networks, the web the story is made of, not redundancy to be varied away.
crux.point: keep the ramble, because the ramble is the consciousness
crux.why: The narration stays glued to Nekohachi's mind, and that mind does not proceed: on the tram it slides from a heckle to why a comedian must not laugh, to protecting a voice he does not drink for, to caterpillars in a ditch and cutworms that, like thieves and like himself, work only at night (p10-p14). The garden returns at every pressure point (p20, p31-p33, p100, p158, p172-p173) and is still what he offers the departing gentlemen at his own gate (p182). A fluent version that breaks this into themed paragraphs, or clarifies the transitions, has rationalised away the man.

crux.for_the_english: keep the embedded summary flat and a little long-winded, keep its pathos unlyrical, and keep Nekohachi's interventions in his own terms (a father should not let the child see it) rather than translating them into the group's critical vocabulary. Let the reader feel the identification before Nekohachi names 悲哀 for himself.
crux.point: let 'The Tiger' stay a clumsy paraphrase, not a set piece
crux.why: Half the story is a second-hand retelling of Kume's tale of a comic actor cast as a tiger whose child finds him weeping in the wings (p48-p90). It would be easy to polish this into a moving story-within-the-story. In the text it arrives as reported talk, interrupted, jargon-dusted (シチュエイション, バック), and judged thin by everyone present. Its power for Nekohachi is precisely that this mediocre fiction has got his life: four sons, a gifted twelve-year-old he has moved to the suburbs to keep away from the yose (p50, p93-p95). Prettify the paraphrase and his response looks disproportionate; sentimentalise his response and the literati's cool verdict loses its sting.

payload.say: Confident on both, from the density of register-marked speech and the sustained tiger mirroring; a different contemporary reception history showing the literati's terms were ordinary unmarked speech in 1918 would soften the first, but not remove it.
